 JoVox: Joint Hierarchical Flow Matching for Lightweight Voxel Generation

Xiangjun Tang    Jianqi Chen    Peter Wonka Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) Affiliation: xiangjun.tang@outlook.com  windvchen@gmail.com  pwonka@gmail.com
Abstract

Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8×8\times higher training throughput, 1/151/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 44 vs. 3232 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11%11\% lower Chamfer distance.

1 Introduction

Voxel generation is an important problem in computer vision. Voxels record where a 3D shape lies in space, giving a lightweight and widely used 3D representation. For example, existing models can turn voxels into fine-grained 3D shapes [30, 31], keeping the structure that the voxels define. Yet generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping this lightweight nature remains an open problem.

Existing methods address this problem in two ways. Latent methods [30, 31] achieve high fidelity by compressing the voxel grid with an autoencoder and generating the latent grid with a generator. The autoencoder is an extra model to train, and the generator still processes every cell of the latent grid, including those in empty space, so the computational cost remains high. Hierarchical methods [9, 33, 27] instead generate a coarse grid first and refine its occupied cells into finer grids, level by level, which keeps the lightweight nature of voxels. However, the coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited. They are thus often plausible but wrong, and the finer levels inherit these errors.

Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level as in hierarchical methods [9, 33, 27]. Such a distribution is hard to model, since the structure of the hierarchy varies across shapes, with finer cells only inside occupied cells. We model it with masked discrete flow matching [11, 7], which unmasks a few cells at each step, at any level of the hierarchy, and grows the hierarchy as cells are unmasked. A coarse cell that is still masked can then be predicted with the finer cells already unmasked nearby. Our framework needs no autoencoder and processes only the cells inside occupied cells, which keeps generation lightweight.

Within this framework, we further introduce two-level prediction and an unmasking strategy. Two-level prediction outputs the cells two levels finer at once, instead of one level finer as in hierarchical methods [9, 6, 27], and thus halves the number of levels that the network processes. We also find that two-level prediction yields voxels of higher fidelity (Section 5.4). Our unmasking strategy remasks the oldest unmasked cells, which were decided with the fewest finer cells around them, so that they are revisited once finer cells are generated. This also corrects the inconsistencies of cells unmasked in the same step [12, 3].

We evaluate our method on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation, where it outperforms current SOTA. In particular, our framework makes training far cheaper than that of TRELLIS.2 [31]. With the same backbone, our framework needs significantly less GPU memory and has 8×8\times higher training throughput (Figure 5), while its voxels remain of higher fidelity, with an 11%11\% lower Chamfer distance.

In summary, our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint hierarchical distribution of voxels while keeping generation lightweight.

  • •

    Two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity, and an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models [12, 3].

  • •

    Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8×8\times higher training throughput, 1/151/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 44 vs. 3232 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11%11\% lower Chamfer distance.

2 Related work

Voxel generation. Voxels are generated as the first stage of many 3D generators [30, 31, 32, 29], or obtained by voxelizing the meshes of 3D generators that produce meshes directly [24, 10]. Methods that generate voxels fall into two groups, dense methods and hierarchical methods.

Dense methods generate every cell of a full grid. TRELLIS [30, 31] compresses the voxels into a compact latent grid with an autoencoder and generates this latent grid, which reaches high fidelity at the cost of training an additional autoencoder. LAS-Diffusion [37] and DVD [32] instead generate the occupancy grid directly. LAS-Diffusion generates the occupancy with continuous diffusion and thresholds the result. DVD treats the occupancy as discrete data and generates it with discrete diffusion. Since all these methods generate every cell, including those in empty space, their cost grows with the cube of the resolution.

Hierarchical methods generate the voxels level by level and refine only occupied cells, which skips empty space. XCube [19] generates a sparse voxel hierarchy, with its own latent diffusion model and autoencoder at each level. Nexus [26] and OctFusion [33] generate the octree with continuous diffusion and threshold the result to decide which cells to refine. Octree Transformer [9] and OAT [6] generate the octree autoregressively, one cell at a time, so the number of forward passes grows with the number of cells. OctGPT [27] generates many cells of a level in parallel by masking. However, it decides the finer cells inside a cell independently and needs many steps at every level. In all these methods, a coarse level is decided from the coarser levels alone. Such a level is only roughly plausible.

We instead learn the joint distribution of all levels, so that finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. Each prediction also outputs the cells two levels finer, instead of one level finer. Like the hierarchical methods above, we refine only occupied cells. We generate the occupancy itself, without an autoencoder. Table 1 summarizes these differences.

Discrete diffusion and flow matching. Masked discrete diffusion models [2, 21, 14, 5] and discrete flow matching [11, 7] generate discrete data by unmasking a masked sequence over several steps, and have been applied to text and image tokens. These data have a fixed size, whereas a voxel hierarchy grows as its cells are unmasked. We extend masked discrete flow matching to such a hierarchy.

When several tokens are unmasked in one step, these models sample them independently, which can make them inconsistent with each other. Some works model the dependence among the tokens unmasked together [8, 12, 34]. Other works choose which tokens to unmask together [28, 3, 15, 20], or remask unmasked tokens so that they can be revised [25]. Our unmasking strategy also remasks, but chooses the oldest unmasked cells, which were decided with the fewest finer cells around them.

3 Discrete flow matching

Discrete flow matching [11, 7] transports samples of a source distribution into samples of a data distribution, along a path indexed by t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. A data sample is a tensor 𝐱=(x1,…,xn)\mathbf{x}=(x^{1},\dots,x^{n}) with nn entries from a finite vocabulary 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The ii-th entry of 𝐱\mathbf{x} is xix^{i}. Throughout, 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} denotes a sample of the data distribution, and 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} a sample of the source distribution, which is a modeling choice. 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} denotes the tensor at tt on the path between 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} and 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}.

A common modeling choice of the source distribution is the masked source [2, 21]. Instead of sampling from a probability distribution, the masked source is a fully masked tensor 𝐱0=(∅,…,∅)\mathbf{x}_{0}=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing), where ∅∉𝒯\varnothing\notin\mathcal{T} is a mask symbol.

Masking. The path from the data to the source is thereby a masking process. Specifically, given 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}, each entry independently keeps its value with probability tt and is masked otherwise. The distribution of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} given 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} is

pt|1​(𝐱t∣𝐱1)=∏i=1n[t​δ​(xti,x1i)+(1−t)​δ​(xti,∅)],p_{t|1}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Big[t\,\delta(x_{t}^{i},x_{1}^{i})+(1-t)\,\delta(x_{t}^{i},\varnothing)\Big], (1)

with δ⁡(a,b)=1\delta(a,b)=1 if a=ba=b and δ⁡(a,b)=0\delta(a,b)=0 otherwise. An entry whose value is in 𝒯\mathcal{T} is called unmasked.

Unmasking. A flow matching model generates data by unmasking. One forward pass of the model, a network with parameters θ\theta, returns probabilities over 𝒯\mathcal{T} for every entry,

pθ​(x1i∣𝐱t,t),i=1,…,n,p_{\theta}(x_{1}^{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t),\qquad i=1,\dots,n, (2)

each approximating the distribution of x1ix_{1}^{i} given 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. For the currently masked entries, these probabilities are predicted considering all already unmasked entries of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}. At each step of generation, a random subset of the masked entries is unmasked, each with a value sampled from its predicted probabilities.

Loss. The model is fitted by minimizing the loss of discrete flow matching [11, 7]. This loss uses the predicted probabilities of both masked and unmasked entries. For the masked path, the loss of entry ii is

ℓi={−log⁡pθ​(x1i∣𝐱t,t)if ​xti=∅,1−pθ​(x1i∣𝐱t,t)otherwise.\ell^{i}=\begin{cases}-\log p_{\theta}(x_{1}^{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t)&\text{if }x_{t}^{i}=\varnothing,\\ 1-p_{\theta}(x_{1}^{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},t)&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3)

The first case is the cross-entropy on a masked entry. The second penalizes a low probability of the unmasked value. The model minimizes

ℒ=∫0111−t​𝔼​[∑iℓi]​𝑑t.\mathcal{L}=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1-t}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{i}\ell^{i}\Big]\,\mathrm{d}t. (4)

4 Method

Given an optional condition cc, such as an image, our task is to generate the occupancy of a shape. We build upon masked discrete flow matching (Section 3) to model the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy. Section 4.1 defines the hierarchy and models its levels jointly, and Section 4.2 introduces two-level prediction. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 describe the network and the training, and Section 4.5 introduces the unmasking strategy for inference.

4.1 Joint hierarchical modeling

A shape is represented by its occupied cells at the levels l=0,…,Ll=0,\dots,L. Level ll is a grid of (4⋅2l)3(4\cdot 2^{l})^{3} cells, and a cell is occupied if the shape surface passes through it. Each cell at level l<Ll<L contains eight cells at level l+1l+1, which we call its children. As in an octree, a cell is identified by its level ll and its position in the grid of level ll. We denote by OlO_{l} the set of occupied cells at level ll and sample O0,…,OLO_{0},\dots,O_{L} from p⁡(O0,…,OL∣c)p(O_{0},\dots,O_{L}\mid c).

Level-by-level generation factorizes this distribution into p⁡(O0∣c)​∏l=1Lp⁡(Ol∣Ol−1,c)p(O_{0}\mid c)\prod_{l=1}^{L}p(O_{l}\mid O_{l-1},c), so each level is decided given only the coarser levels. We instead learn the joint distribution of all levels with the masked discrete flow matching of Section 3, so that a coarse cell can be predicted given finer cells that are already generated.

Occupancies. Without loss of generality, we start with a straightforward choice of the entries xix^{i} of Section 3 for hierarchical modeling. We define the entry xi∈𝐱1x^{i}\in\mathbf{x}_{1} as the occupancy of a cell. The occupancy is 11 if the cell is occupied and 00 otherwise, so that xi∈𝒯={0,1}x^{i}\in\mathcal{T}=\{0,1\}. During discrete flow matching, an occupancy can also be masked, and a masked occupancy is the mask symbol ∅\varnothing of Section 3.

Masking. The data sample 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} contains the occupancies of the cells at level 00 and of the children of occupied cells, and it determines O0,…,OLO_{0},\dots,O_{L}. As in Section 3, we obtain an intermediate state by masking some occupancies of 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}. Masking the occupancy of a cell also removes all cells inside it, since their occupancies would reveal the masked occupancy. We mask the levels J={0,…,L}J=\{0,\dots,L\} in order, from the coarsest to the finest. At level ll, each occupancy keeps its value with probability tlt_{l} and is masked otherwise. The resulting intermediate state 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, with 𝐭=(tl)l∈J\mathbf{t}=(t_{l})_{l\in J}, thus contains the occupancies of 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} whose cells are not removed, and each of these occupancies keeps its value or is masked. 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}} follows

p𝐭|1​(𝐱𝐭∣𝐱1)=∏l∈J∏i∈𝒞l​(𝐱𝐭)[tl​δ​(xtli,x1i)+(1−tl)​δ​(xtli,∅)],p_{\mathbf{t}|1}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})=\prod_{l\in J}\,\prod_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}})}\Big[t_{l}\,\delta(x_{t_{l}}^{i},x_{1}^{i})+(1-t_{l})\,\delta(x_{t_{l}}^{i},\varnothing)\Big], (5)

where 𝒞l​(𝐱𝐭)\mathcal{C}_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}) is the set of occupancies at level ll in 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}. The number of occupancies thus depends on which cells are known to be occupied. It differs between shapes, and even for the same shape it changes as the shape is built during discrete flow matching.

Unmasking. Given 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, 𝐭\mathbf{t} and cc, the model processes each cell whose occupancy is in 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}} and returns probabilities over 𝒯\mathcal{T} for its occupancy,

pθ​(x1i∣𝐱𝐭,𝐭,c),i∈𝒞l​(𝐱𝐭),l∈J.p_{\theta}(x_{1}^{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}},\mathbf{t},c),\qquad i\in\mathcal{C}_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}),\ l\in J. (6)

Generation starts from 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. At each step, we choose masked occupancies at any level at random (Section 4.5) and unmask them by sampling their values from the probabilities of Equation (6). Once a cell at level l<Ll<L is known to be occupied, we add masked occupancies of its children to 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, so the hierarchy grows as occupancies are unmasked. Since occupancies at any level can be unmasked, some occupancies at a coarse level can still be masked when occupancies at finer levels in nearby cells are already unmasked.

4.2 Two-level prediction

Hierarchical methods such as Octree Transformer [9] define the occupancy code of a cell as the occupancy of its eight children, which has 8 bits. They process a cell to predict its occupancy code, one level finer, instead of its own occupancy as in Section 4.1. We call this single-level prediction. In our framework, single-level prediction uses the formulation of Section 4.1 with occupancy codes in place of occupancies. The entries xi∈𝒯={0,1}8x^{i}\in\mathcal{T}=\{0,1\}^{8} are the occupancy codes at the levels J={0,…,L−1}J=\{0,\dots,L-1\}. The data sample 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} contains the occupancy codes of the cells at level 00 and of the occupied cells at the levels 1,…,L−11,\dots,L-1. We mask the occupancy codes as in Section 4.1 to obtain 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, where 𝒞l​(𝐱𝐭)\mathcal{C}_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}) is now the set of occupancy codes at level ll in 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}. Once a cell at the levels 1,…,L−11,\dots,L-1 is known to be occupied, we add its masked occupancy code to 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}.

In two-level prediction, the model instead processes a cell uu at level l≤L−2l\leq L-2 to predict the occupancy of its 4×4×44\times 4\times 4 cells two levels finer, at level l+2l+2 (Figure 2 (a)). One possible way is to use the occupancy of these cells as one entry, but such an entry would take 2642^{64} values, which is prohibitively large. We therefore split the occupancy of these cells into eight 8-bit occupancy codes, one for each child of uu, each giving the occupancy of the eight cells at level l+2l+2 inside that child. For a cell uu, the model thus takes these eight occupancy codes, masked or unmasked, as input and outputs eight distributions of Equation (6), each over the 282^{8} values of an occupancy code, instead of one distribution over 2642^{64} values.

Specifically, we take LL to be even and let the cells uu lie at the even levels 0,2,…,L−20,2,\dots,L-2, so that the entries are the occupancy codes at the odd levels J={1,3,…,L−1}J=\{1,3,\dots,L-1\}. The data sample 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1} contains the 8-bit occupancy codes of the eight children of every cell uu at level 00 and of every occupied cell uu at the levels 2,…,L−22,\dots,L-2. We mask the occupancy codes as in single-level prediction to obtain 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}. Once a cell uu at the levels 2,…,L−22,\dots,L-2 is known to be occupied, we add the masked occupancy codes of its eight children to 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}. The model thus processes each cell uu at level 00 and each cell uu known to be occupied. Two-level prediction thus processes cells at only half of the levels of single-level prediction, so training is faster (Section 5.4).

4.3 Network

The network is a transformer that takes one token for each cell uu of Section 4.2, as illustrated in Figure 2 (b).

As in Figure 2 (a), we number the children of a cell 1,…,81,\dots,8 in a fixed order. We write aja_{j} for the value of the jj-th child of uu and aj,ba_{j,b} for the value of the bb-th child of this child. A value is 11 if the cell is occupied, 00 if it is empty, and ∅\varnothing if the occupancy code of the jj-th child is masked. The token hh of uu embeds these values, the level ll and the position rr of uu as

h=∑j=18ej​(aj)+W​[∑b=18eb​(aj,b)]j=18+emblevel​(l)+embpos​(r),h=\sum_{j=1}^{8}e_{j}(a_{j})+W\Big[\sum_{b=1}^{8}e_{b}(a_{j,b})\Big]_{j=1}^{8}+\mathrm{emb}_{\text{level}}(l)+\mathrm{emb}_{\text{pos}}(r), (7)

where eme_{m} is a learned embedding of the values {0,1,∅}\{0,1,\varnothing\} for the mm-th child of a cell, used both for the children of uu, as eje_{j}, and for the cells inside each child, as ebe_{b}. The first term embeds the eight children. The second sums the embeddings of the eight cells inside each child. The eight sums are concatenated in the order of the children, written [⋅]j=18[\cdot]_{j=1}^{8}, and a learned linear map WW maps them to one vector. The level embedding is one learned vector per level. The point r∈[0,1)3r\in[0,1)^{3} is the center of uu in a frame shared by all levels. embpos​(r)\mathrm{emb}_{\text{pos}}(r) is the point embedding of 3DShape2VecSet [36].

The transformer has the same architecture as the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 [31]. It processes the tokens of all levels in one sequence, with full self-attention and 3D rotary position embeddings of rr. When cc is an image, we feed its DINOv3 features [22] to every block through cross-attention. We embed each tlt_{l} with its own time embedding embtl\mathrm{emb}_{t}^{\,l}, and condition all tokens on the sum ∑l∈Jembtl​(tl)\sum_{l\in J}\mathrm{emb}_{t}^{\,l}(t_{l}) through adaptive layer normalization in every block.

4.4 Training

During training, we first draw tlt_{l} for each level l∈Jl\in J and then draw 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}} from Equation (5). We draw the tlt_{l} of different levels independently, so the network is trained on any combination of fractions across levels. The intermediate states 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}} produced by any unmasking strategy therefore lie within the training distribution. To train the network more where its predictions are least certain, we draw small tlt_{l} more often, following the distribution given in Section B in the appendix.

Finer levels have far more occupancy codes than coarser ones, so a loss summed over all occupancy codes would be dominated by the finer levels. We therefore first average the loss over the occupancy codes of each level, and then average over the levels. With J⁡(𝐱𝐭)J(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}) the set of levels that have occupancy codes in 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, the loss is

ℒours=𝔼⁡[1|J⁡(𝐱𝐭)|​∑l∈J⁡(𝐱𝐭)1(1−tl)​|𝒞l​(𝐱𝐭)|​∑i∈𝒞l​(𝐱𝐭)ℓi],\mathcal{L}_{\text{ours}}=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{|J(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}})|}\sum_{l\in J(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}})}\frac{1}{(1-t_{l})\,|\mathcal{C}_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}})|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}})}\ell^{i}\Big], (8)

where ℓi\ell^{i} is the loss of Equation (3), and each level is weighted by 1/(1−tl)1/(1-t_{l}) as in Equation (4).

4.5 Unmasking strategy

Occupancy codes unmasked in the same step are sampled independently, each from its predicted probabilities, so they may be inconsistent with each other [8, 12, 34, 3]. Some samplers for masked generation correct such inconsistencies by remasking unmasked entries, so that these entries are predicted again [25]. Our strategy also remasks, and chooses the occupancy codes to remask by when they were unmasked. Occupancy codes unmasked early are sampled given few unmasked occupancy codes. This holds in particular for coarse occupancy codes, which are unmasked before most finer occupancy codes exist. Our strategy therefore remasks the oldest unmasked occupancy codes at each step, so that they are predicted again given the occupancy codes unmasked after them, including finer occupancy codes in nearby cells.

Generation starts from 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} and runs for NN steps k=0,…,N−1k=0,\dots,N-1. At step kk, the target fraction of unmasked occupancy codes at level l∈Jl\in J is given by the schedule

κl​(k)=min⁡(k/Nl,1)ρ,\kappa_{l}(k)=\min(k/N_{l},1)^{\rho}, (9)

which reaches 11 at k=Nl≤Nk=N_{l}\leq N. Finer occupancy codes are added as coarser ones are unmasked, so we let the schedules of coarser levels reach 11 earlier, N1≤N3≤⋯≤NL−1=NN_{1}\leq N_{3}\leq\dots\leq N_{L-1}=N. Early in generation, with few occupancy codes unmasked, the predictions are least certain, so occupancy codes unmasked in the same step are most likely to be inconsistent with each other. We therefore use ρ>1\rho>1, so that κl\kappa_{l} grows slowly at first and quickly later.

Each step kk does three things in order. First, for k≥1k\geq 1, each level remasks its oldest unmasked occupancy codes, so that its fraction of unmasked occupancy codes goes back to about κl​(k−1)\kappa_{l}(k-1). When an occupancy code is remasked, the cells that it marked as occupied are no longer known to be occupied. As in Section 4.1, the occupancy codes of all cells inside them are then removed from 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}. Second, the network predicts all masked occupancy codes in 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, with each tlt_{l} set to the fraction of unmasked occupancy codes at level ll. Third, each level unmasks masked occupancy codes chosen at random, so that its fraction rises to about κl​(k+1)\kappa_{l}(k+1). To unmask an occupancy code, we sample its value from the probabilities predicted in the second step, at temperature τ\tau. At τ=0\tau=0, we take the most probable value. Under the schedule, a very large number of occupancy codes at level L−1L-1 would be unmasked in step N−1N-1, and these would likely be inconsistent with each other. To alleviate this, we add a few extra steps after step N−1N-1 and unmask these occupancy codes evenly over step N−1N-1 and the extra steps. The extra steps do not remask. See Section B in the appendix for details.

5 Experiments

We evaluate our framework on image-conditioned generation (Section 5.1) and unconditional generation (Section 5.2), measure its efficiency (Section 5.3), and ablate its designs (Section 5.4). All shapes are represented by their 64364^{3} surface occupancy, the finest level of a hierarchy with L=4L=4. We also show shapes generated at a higher resolution of 2563256^{3} by our framework with L=6L=6 in Section A of the appendix. We run all baselines in Sections 5.1 and 5.2 with their official weights and settings, and evaluate all methods on the same test data with the same metrics in each task. Details of the data and metrics are provided in the appendix.

5.1 Image-conditioned generation

Data. We train on 174,528174{,}528 assets of TRELLIS-500K [30] and test on 1,0001{,}000 objects of Toys4k [23], which are unseen during training. The condition is a rendered view of each asset.

Baselines. We compare with TRELLIS.2 [31], the state of the art, and with TRELLIS [30], DVD [32], Direct3D-S2 [29], TripoSG [10] and TripoSR [24]. Voxels are often used to generate meshes, so we evaluate both the voxels and the meshes of each method. TRELLIS, DVD, TRELLIS.2, our framework and Direct3D-S2 generate 64364^{3} voxels. For the first four, we obtain the meshes by passing the voxels through the mesh stage of TRELLIS.2, which generates a mesh from 64364^{3} voxels. Direct3D-S2 refines its voxels into a mesh with its own second stage, and we evaluate this mesh. TripoSG and TripoSR generate meshes directly, and their voxel metrics use these meshes voxelized at 64364^{3}.

Metrics. We first align each generated shape to its ground truth in orientation and scale, and then compare it with the ground truth. On the voxels, we report the voxel Chamfer distance (CDV{}_{\text{V}}) and the voxel IoU, which measure geometric accuracy. A few misplaced voxels barely change these two metrics but produce visible artifacts, so we also report the LPIPS (LPIPSV{}_{\text{V}}) and DINOv2 [17] similarity (DINOV{}_{\text{V}}) between renderings of the generated and ground-truth voxels, which measure perceptual similarity. On the meshes, we report (i) CDshell{}_{\text{shell}}, the Chamfer distance between the outer surfaces, which measures geometric accuracy, (ii) LPIPSN{}_{\text{N}} and CLIPN{}_{\text{N}} [18] on rendered normal maps, which measure perceptual similarity, and (iii) the Uni3D [38] similarity of point clouds sampled on the meshes, which measures semantic similarity.

Results. As shown in Table 2, our framework achieves the best value on every voxel metric. Compared with TRELLIS.2, its voxels have an 11%11\% lower Chamfer distance and an IoU of 0.4160.416 against 0.4020.402, and their renderings have the highest perceptual similarity to the ground truth. Since TRELLIS, DVD, TRELLIS.2 and our framework share one mesh stage, their meshes differ only in the voxels they start from. Our voxels thus lead to a 22%22\% lower CDshell{}_{\text{shell}} than those of TRELLIS.2 and to the lowest LPIPSN{}_{\text{N}} (Figure 3).

5.2 Unconditional generation

Data. We use the chair, airplane, table and rifle categories of ShapeNet [4], with the training and test splits of LAS-Diffusion [37]. The test split of each category, voxelized at 64364^{3}, serves as its reference set.

Baselines. We compare with LAS-Diffusion, OctFusion [33], OctGPT [27] and XCube [19]. XCube releases models only for chair and airplane, so we compare with it on these two categories. LAS-Diffusion generates 64364^{3} occupancy, and XCube generates a sparse 5123512^{3} occupancy, which we max-pool to 64364^{3}. OctFusion and OctGPT output a 32332^{3} occupancy and a mesh. We evaluate both outputs of these two methods, voxelizing the meshes at 64364^{3} in the same way as the reference sets. Rows that use the 32332^{3} occupancy are marked in the tables.

Metrics. Unconditional samples have no corresponding ground truth, so we compare the generated set of each category with its reference set. We report the 1-NNA, the coverage (COV) and the minimum matching distance (MMD) [1, 35], which measure distribution similarity, diversity and fidelity, respectively, all computed with the Chamfer distance between voxel centers. We also report FIDV{}_{\text{V}} on PointNet++ features of Point-E [16], and FIDVD{}_{\text{VD}} and KIDVD{}_{\text{VD}} on DINOv2 features of voxel renderings, which measure the distance between the generated and reference distributions in a 3D feature space and an image feature space, respectively.

Results. As shown in Table 3, our framework achieves the best value on all six metrics, averaged over the four categories. Its FIDV{}_{\text{V}} is 80%80\% lower and its FIDVD{}_{\text{VD}} is 64%64\% lower than the best baseline values. OctFusion, OctGPT and XCube are hierarchical methods, whose coarse levels are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited. Our framework learns the joint distribution of all levels and outperforms OctFusion and OctGPT on the four categories and XCube on chair and airplane. Table 7 in the appendix gives the results of each category. Figure 4 shows chairs generated by our framework, with fine and complex structures.

5.3 Efficiency

We compare one training step (a forward pass, a backward pass and an optimizer update) of our network and of the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 with the same backbone. Both run on one A100 GPU with 80 GB, with gradient checkpointing, fp32 master weights and bf16 mixed precision. As shown in Figure 5, at a batch size of 3232 our framework needs 29.029.0 GB of GPU memory instead of 47.347.3 GB and has 8×8\times higher training throughput, and it can be trained with batch sizes at which TRELLIS.2 runs out of memory. Since the two networks share the backbone, these differences in memory and throughput come from the number of cells they process. TRELLIS.2 processes all 4,0964{,}096 cells of its 16316^{3} latent grid for every shape, including those in empty space, while our network processes only the cells that have a token. In a training state 𝐱𝐭\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{t}}, which is partly masked, 273273 cells have a token on average. A complete shape, in which no occupancy code is masked as at the end of generation, has 579579 on average over the Toys4k test set. One forward pass of our network therefore takes on average about 1/151/15 of the FLOPs of the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 (0.820.82 vs. 12.212.2 TFLOPs).

To measure the cost of full training, we train our framework on four H100 GPUs with a batch size of 256256. TRELLIS and TRELLIS.2 are trained with the same batch size on 6464 A100 GPUs and 3232 H100 GPUs, respectively, 1616 and 88 times as many GPUs as we use. After about two days of training (8080K steps), our framework surpasses TRELLIS, which is trained for 400400K steps, on every metric of Section 5.1. After about two and a half days, it matches TRELLIS.2 (Table 9 in the appendix), whose paper does not report the number of training steps. Our framework also generates the voxels faster than the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 (Table 6 in the appendix).

5.4 Ablation studies

We conduct ablation studies on image-conditioned generation on Toys4k.

Two-level prediction and joint hierarchical modeling. We compare our framework with two variants in Table 4. The single-level variant uses single-level prediction (Section 4.2) and the two-level variant uses two-level prediction, and both generate the hierarchy level by level. By contrast, ours extends the two-level variant with joint hierarchical modeling. All three share the network architecture and the training data, and are trained for the same number of steps, fewer than those used for our model in Section 5.1. As shown in Table 4, the two-level variant improves every metric over the single-level variant. Compared with the two-level variant, our framework lowers the voxel Chamfer distance by 22%22\% and CDshell{}_{\text{shell}} by 32%32\%, and improves every metric. In addition, two-level prediction makes training faster, since the network processes fewer tokens. With both variants on four A100 GPUs at a batch size of 256256, one training step of the two-level variant takes 4.034.03 s, compared with 8.968.96 s for the single-level variant, a 2.2×2.2\times speedup.

Unmasking strategy. We compare our unmasking strategy with other samplers, all applied to our model of Section 5.1. MDLM [21] does not remask. ReMDM [25] remasks unmasked occupancy codes chosen at random, and its confidence-based variant ReMDM-conf [25] remasks the less confident ones with a higher probability. MaskGIT [5] unmasks the most probable occupancy codes first and does not remask. Unlike these samplers, our strategy chooses the occupancy codes to remask by when they were unmasked. An occupancy code unmasked earlier is predicted given fewer finer occupancy codes in nearby cells, so its prediction is less certain. Our strategy therefore remasks the oldest unmasked occupancy codes, so that they are revisited once finer occupancy codes are unmasked. As shown in Table 5, our strategy gives the lowest voxel Chamfer distance and the highest IoU among all samplers.

6 Limitations and future work

A limitation of our model is the size of its training set. Due to limited training resources, we train it on about 175175K assets, less than a quarter of the roughly 800800K assets used to train TRELLIS.2 [31]. While our model, with the data augmentation described in the appendix, still outperforms TRELLIS.2 in generalization to the unseen objects of Toys4k, we expect more training data to further improve it. Besides, like other masked discrete flow matching models, our model unmasks multiple occupancy codes independently in one step, which can make them inconsistent with each other [8, 12, 34, 3]. Our unmasking strategy is designed to reduce such inconsistencies, and exploring better unmasking strategies may further improve the quality of the generated voxels.

In future work, we plan to apply our framework to generating large scenes with multiple objects and long sequences of 3D shapes. Both contain far more voxels than a single object, and our framework keeps their training lightweight by processing only the cells inside occupied cells.

7 Conclusion

We presented JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, so that finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. Within this framework, two-level prediction halves the number of levels that the network processes and yields voxels of higher fidelity, and our unmasking strategy revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated. Our framework outperforms the baselines on unconditional and image-conditioned generation, while its training is far cheaper than that of TRELLIS.2. Our results thus show that voxels can be generated with both clearly improved fidelity and drastically improved efficiency.

A Generation at 2563256^{3}

Figure 6 shows shapes generated at 2563256^{3} from input images by our framework with L=6L=6 (Section B).

B Implementation details

The experiments in Section 5 use L=4L=4, so the finest level is a grid of 64364^{3} cells. The tokens come from the cells at level 00 and the occupied cells at level 22, with grids of 434^{3} and 16316^{3} cells, and the occupancy codes are at levels 11 and 33. The 2563256^{3} shapes in Section A and on the project webpage are generated by a model with L=6L=6, where the tokens come from the cells at level 00 and the occupied cells at levels 22 and 44, and the occupancy codes are at levels 11, 33 and 55. For this model, we add the level embedding emblevel​(4)\mathrm{emb}_{\text{level}}(4) and the embedding embt 5\mathrm{emb}_{t}^{\,5} of t5t_{5}, initialize all other weights from the model with L=4L=4, and train it for 3232K further steps on four GPUs.

The transformer has 1.541.54B parameters in 3030 blocks of width 15361536 with 1212 heads. The image encoder is a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 at a resolution of 512×512512\times 512. The condition is dropped with probability 0.10.1 during training, and classifier-free guidance at scale 1.51.5 is applied to the logits during sampling.

We train with AdamW [13] at a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} and a batch size of 256256 on four GPUs, and keep an exponential moving average of the weights. For data augmentation, the condition image is randomly perturbed in brightness, saturation, contrast, hue and gamma, and the occupancy is rotated by a random multiple of 90∘90^{\circ} about the vertical axis. We draw tl=vl2t_{l}=v_{l}^{2} with vl∼𝒰⁡(0,1)v_{l}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1).

In the unmasking strategy of Section 4.5, we remask at the levels one after another at each step, from the coarsest to the finest, so that we count the unmasked occupancy codes at a finer level only after remasking at the coarser levels has removed some of them. At step k≥1k\geq 1, at each level ll with κl​(k)<1\kappa_{l}(k)<1, we remask up to round⁡((1−κl​(k−1)/κl​(k))​n)\operatorname{round}\big((1-\kappa_{l}(k-1)/\kappa_{l}(k))\,n\big) occupancy codes, rounded half to even, where nn is the number of all unmasked occupancy codes at level ll. We do not remask an occupancy code unmasked at step k−1k-1, since no prediction has yet been made given it, nor an occupancy code unmasked in a step in which no other occupancy code, at any level, was unmasked. Among the other unmasked occupancy codes, we remask those last unmasked earliest, with ties broken at random, or all of them if there are fewer. For the prediction, we set tlt_{l} to 00 at a level that has no occupancy codes. After the prediction, we unmask only occupancy codes predicted at this step, and occupancy codes added after an unmasking are first predicted at the next step and are not counted below. At a level ll with κl​(k−1)=1\kappa_{l}(k-1)=1, we unmask all of its masked occupancy codes. At any other level ll with masked occupancy codes, we unmask the proportion (κl​(k+1)−κl​(k−1))/(1−κl​(k−1))\big(\kappa_{l}(k+1)-\kappa_{l}(k-1)\big)/\big(1-\kappa_{l}(k-1)\big) of them, rounded up and at least one, chosen at random, where κl​(−1)=0\kappa_{l}(-1)=0. From step N−1N-1 on, we instead unmask the proportion 1/(N+Nf−k)1/(N+N_{\text{f}}-k) of the masked occupancy codes at level L−1L-1 at step kk, also rounded up and at least one, so that they are unmasked evenly over step N−1N-1 and NfN_{\text{f}} extra steps, and we do not remask in the extra steps.

For image-conditioned generation, the sampler uses N=72N=72, Nf=8N_{\text{f}}=8, N1=0.8​NN_{1}=0.8N, ρ=2\rho=2 and τ=0\tau=0, so a generation takes 8080 steps. For unconditional generation, it uses τ=1\tau=1, with N=288N=288 for chair and table and N=72N=72 for airplane and rifle.

Table 6 reports the time and the peak GPU memory of generating the voxels. Our framework generates the voxels faster than the voxel stage of TRELLIS.2 at every batch size.

C Data and evaluation details

Data. The 174,528174{,}528 training assets come from the Sketchfab, ABO, 3D-FUTURE and HSSD parts of TRELLIS-500K [30], about 35%35\% of the full dataset. The condition of a training asset is a rendered view at an elevation between −10∘-10^{\circ} and 30∘30^{\circ}, and each Toys4k test object has one condition view at a similar elevation. On ShapeNet, each category is evaluated separately on its test split, and its reference set has as many shapes as the generated set.

Alignment. Methods and datasets differ in their orientation and scale conventions. We therefore align each generated shape to its ground truth by picking the one of the 2424 axis-aligned rotations that minimizes the voxel Chamfer distance and refining it with a scale-aware ICP.

Voxel metrics. For LPIPSV{}_{\text{V}} and DINOV{}_{\text{V}}, we render the aligned voxels and the ground-truth voxels from six views and average the LPIPS and the cosine similarity of DINOv2 features over the views. For Direct3D-S2, the voxel metrics use the 64364^{3} voxels of its dense first stage, and for TripoSG and TripoSR, they use their voxelized meshes.

Mesh metrics. The meshes of Direct3D-S2, TripoSG and TripoSR are aligned to the ground truth in the same way. CDshell{}_{\text{shell}} is the Chamfer distance between the outer surfaces of the two meshes. LPIPSN{}_{\text{N}} and CLIPN{}_{\text{N}} compare normal maps rendered from four views. Uni3D is the similarity between the Uni3D embeddings of point clouds sampled on the two meshes.

ShapeNet metrics. FIDV{}_{\text{V}} is computed on points of the voxels. FIDVD{}_{\text{VD}} and KIDVD{}_{\text{VD}} use renderings of the voxels from six views.

D Additional ablations

This section measures two choices of Section B on the first 200200 objects of Toys4k, with the unmasking strategy of Section 4.5.

Exponential moving average of the weights. For our model, the moving average improves CDV{}_{\text{V}} from 0.012150.01215 to 0.011930.01193 and CDshell{}_{\text{shell}} from 0.503×10−30.503\times 10^{-3} to 0.446×10−30.446\times 10^{-3}. It also improves LPIPSN{}_{\text{N}} from 0.17580.1758 to 0.17140.1714.

Augmentation. We train the same model with and without the augmentation of Section B and compare the two after the same number of training steps (Table 8). Augmentation improves CDV{}_{\text{V}}, CDshell{}_{\text{shell}}, LPIPSN{}_{\text{N}}, CLIPN{}_{\text{N}} and Uni3D.
